label: Sayings CX–CXXXV
paragraphs: CX. One of his pupils, who seemed drawn to the Cynic life, asked him what kind of man the Cynic ought to be and what our preconception of the thing should be. He said: We will look into it at leisure. But this much I can tell you: the man who takes up so great a thing without God is under the anger of God, and wants nothing else than to disgrace himself in public. For in a well-run house, too, no one comes forward and says to himself, "I ought to be the manager." If he does, the master turns, sees him giving orders in his high-handed way, drags him out, and has him flogged. It is the same in this great city. For here too there is a master of the house who assigns each thing its place. "You are the sun. You have the power, as you go your round, to make the year and the seasons, to make the crops grow and feed them, to raise the winds and calm them, and to warm the bodies of men in due measure. Go, make your round, and so set all things moving, from the greatest to the smallest. You have the power to lead the army against Troy: be Agamemnon. You have the power to fight Hector in single combat: be Achilles." But if Thersites had come forward and claimed the command, either he would not have got it, or if he had, he would have disgraced himself before many witnesses.

CXI. For you must know this: other men have their walls and their houses and the dark to shelter them when they do anything of that kind, and they have many ways to hide. A man shuts his door and stations someone outside his bedroom: "If anyone comes, say, 'He is out; he is busy.'" But the Cynic, in place of all these, must have his self-respect to shelter him. Otherwise he will be disgraced, naked and in the open air. This is his house, this is his door, this is the guard at his bedroom, this is his darkness.

CXII. Death? Let it come when it will, whether of the whole or of some part. Exile? And where can anyone throw me out to? Outside the universe he cannot. Wherever I go, there is the sun, there the moon, there the stars, dreams, omens, converse with the gods.

CXIII. Then, even when he is prepared in this way, the true Cynic cannot be content with that. He must know that he has been sent as a messenger from Zeus to men, to show them about good and evil: that they have gone astray and are looking for the essence of good and evil where it is not, and give no thought to where it is. And he must know that, like Diogenes when he was led off to Philip after the battle of Chaeronea, he is a scout. For the Cynic really is a scout, to find out what is friendly to men and what is hostile. He must scout carefully and come back and report the truth, not so stricken by fear that he points out enemies who are not there, and not in any other way thrown into confusion or disorder by impressions.

CXIV. "And how is it possible for a man who has nothing, who is naked, without house or hearth, unwashed, without a slave, without a city, to live a life that flows smoothly?" Look, God has sent you a man to show you in fact that it is possible. "Look at me. I have no house, no city, no property, no slave. I sleep on the ground. I have no wife, no children, no governor's residence, only earth and sky and one poor cloak. And what do I lack? Am I not free of grief? Am I not free of fear? Am I not free? When did I ever blame God or man? When did I accuse anyone? Has any of you seen me with a gloomy face? And how do I meet the men you fear and admire? Is it not as slaves? Who, when he sees me, does not think he is looking at his own king and master?"
CXV. Think it over more carefully. Know yourself. Consult the divine. Do not attempt it without God.

CXVI. "But marriage and children," the young man said, "will the Cynic take these on as a chief duty?" "If you give me a city of wise men," he said, "perhaps no one will readily come to the Cynic life at all. For whose sake would he take up this way of living? But suppose he does: nothing will prevent him from marrying and having children. For his wife will be another like him, and his father-in-law another like him, and his children will be brought up in the same way. But with things as they are now, as if drawn up for battle, should the Cynic not be undistracted, wholly given to the service of God, able to go about among men, not tied down by the duties of a private man or tangled in relationships which he cannot break and still keep the role of a good and noble man, and cannot keep without destroying the messenger, the scout, the herald of the gods?"

CXVII. Ask me too, if you like, whether he will take part in public life. Fool, are you looking for a greater public life than the one he takes part in? Or is a man to come forward among the Athenians and speak about revenues and supplies, when he ought to be talking with all men, Athenians and Corinthians and Romans alike, not about supplies or revenues or peace or war, but about happiness and unhappiness, good fortune and bad, slavery and freedom? When a man is taking part in so great a public life, do you ask me whether he will take part in public life? Ask me too whether he will hold office. Again I will tell you: fool, what office is greater than the one he holds?

CXVIII. Such a man does also need a certain kind of body. For if he comes forward consumptive, thin and pale, his witness no longer carries the same weight. He must not only show laymen, by displaying what belongs to his soul, that it is possible to be a good and noble man without the things they admire; he must also show by his body that a simple, frugal life in the open air does no harm to the body either. "Look, I and my body are witnesses to this as well." That is what Diogenes did: he went about glowing with health, and his body alone turned people's heads. But a Cynic who is pitied looks like a beggar; everyone turns away, everyone takes offense. He must not look dirty either, so as not to drive people off in that way too; his very roughness should be clean and attractive.

CXIX. For kings and tyrants, their guards and their weapons made it possible to rebuke certain people and to punish wrongdoers, even when they were bad men themselves. To the Cynic it is not weapons and guards but his conscience that gives this authority. When you see that he has kept watch over mankind and worked hard for them; that he has gone to sleep pure, and sleep has left him purer still; that whatever he has thought, he has thought as a friend of the gods, as a servant, as one who shares in the rule of Zeus; that everywhere he has ready at hand "Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny," and "If this is what pleases the gods, so be it": why should he not have the courage to speak freely to his own brothers, to his children, in a word to his kin?

CXX. Does a philosopher invite people to a lecture? Does he not, as the sun draws its own nourishment to itself, draw to himself those who will be helped? What doctor invites anyone to come and be treated by him? Though I hear that nowadays in Rome the doctors do send invitations; in my time they were the ones invited. "I invite you to come and hear that you are in a bad way, that you take care of everything except what you should, that you do not know what is good and what is evil, and that you are unhappy and unfortunate." A charming invitation. And yet if the philosopher's words do not bring this home, they are dead, and so is the speaker.

CXXI. Gentlemen, the philosopher's school is a doctor's office. You ought not to leave it in pleasure but in pain. For you do not come in healthy: one has put out his shoulder, another has an abscess, another a fistula, another a headache. And then am I to sit and recite little thoughts and clever phrases to you, so that you will praise me and go out, one carrying his shoulder just as he brought it in, another with his head in the same state, another his fistula, another his abscess? Is it for this that young men are to leave home, and leave their parents and friends and relatives and their bit of property: to say "Bravo!" while you recite clever phrases?
CXXII. And if anyone is unhappy, remember that he is unhappy because of himself. For God made all men for happiness, for steadiness.

CXXIII. Shall we not wean ourselves at last, and remember what we heard from the philosophers? Unless we listened to them as if they were chanting spells: that this universe is one city, and the substance out of which it has been made is one; that there must be a cycle, and a giving way of some things to others; that some things must be dissolved and others come into being, some stay where they are and others move. And everything is full of friends: first gods, and then men too, who by nature have been made to belong to one another.

CXXIV. Heracles married, too, where the moment seemed right to him, and had children, and left his children behind without groaning or longing for them, and not as if he were leaving them orphans. For he knew that no human being is an orphan, but that all have, always and without a break, the father who cares for them. For it was not as mere talk that he had heard that Zeus is the father of men; he thought him his own father and called him so, and did what he did looking to him. And so he was able to live happily everywhere.

CXXV. Do you not know that the thing is a campaign? One man must stand guard, another go out to scout, another go out to fight. It is not possible for all to be in the same place, and it would not be better. But you neglect to carry out the general's orders, and complain when you are given a rougher one; and you do not see what you are making of the army, so far as it depends on you: that if everyone copies you, no one will dig a trench, no one will put up a palisade, no one will keep watch, no one will face danger, and each will be seen to be useless as a soldier. So it is here too. Each man's life is a kind of campaign, and a long and varied one. You must keep the soldier's part and do each thing at the general's nod; if possible, divining what he wants. For this general is not like the other, either in strength or in excellence of character.

CXXVI. Have you forgotten again what you came for? Do you not know that a good and noble man does nothing for the sake of appearances, but for the sake of having acted rightly? "Is there no prize, then?" Are you looking for a greater prize for a good man than doing what is noble and just? At Olympia no one asks for anything else; you think it is enough to have been crowned an Olympic victor. Does it seem to you so small and worthless a thing to be good and noble and happy?
CXXVII. A man should be unhappy on no one's account, but happy on account of all, and most of all on account of God, who made us for this.

CXXVIII. Come, did Diogenes love no one, he who was so gentle and so kind to mankind that he gladly took on so many labors and hardships of the body for the common good of men? But how did he love? As a servant of Zeus should: caring for them, and at the same time subject to God.
CXXIX. I was born for what is good for me; I was not born for what is evil.

CXXX. Remind yourself that what you love is mortal, that what you love is nothing of your own. It has been given to you for the present, not beyond recall and not forever, but like a fig or a bunch of grapes, at the appointed season of the year. "But those are words of bad omen." Do you call anything of bad omen except what signifies some evil? Cowardice is of bad omen, and meanness of spirit, mourning, grief, shamelessness: those are the words of bad omen. But do you tell me that a word is of bad omen when it signifies a work of nature? Then say it is of bad omen for the ears of grain to be reaped; for it signifies the destruction of the ears. But not of the universe. Say that the falling of the leaves is of bad omen too, and the fresh fig becoming a dried fig, and grapes becoming raisins. For all these are changes from what was before into something else: not destruction, but an appointed arrangement and governance. Going abroad is this: a small change. Death is this: a greater change, from what is now, not into what is not, but into what is not now. "So I will no longer exist?" You will not; but something else will, which the universe now needs. For you too came to be, not when you wished, but when the universe had need.

CXXXI. That is why the good and noble man, remembering who he is and where he has come from and by whom he was made, attends to this one thing only: how to fill his own place in good order and in obedience to God. "Do you want me to go on existing? Then I will, as a free man, as a noble one, as you wished; for you made me unhindered in what is mine. But have you no further need of me? May it be well with you. Until now I stayed on your account and no one else's, and now I obey you and go." "How do you go?" "Again, as you wished: as a free man, as your servant, as one who has understood your commands and your prohibitions."

CXXXII. "Whatever place and post you put in my hands, as Socrates says, I will die ten thousand times before I abandon it. And where do you want me to be? In Rome, or Athens, or Thebes, or on Gyara? Only remember me there. If you send me where men cannot live in keeping with nature, I will depart, not in disobedience to you, but because you are sounding the recall for me. I am not deserting you. Far from it. But I see that you have no need of me."

CXXXIII. If you are on Gyara, do not picture the life in Rome, and all the pleasures a man had who lived there, and all he would have if he went back. Set yourself on this instead: how a man who lives on Gyara should live on Gyara with vigor. And if you are in Rome, do not picture the life in Athens; study only the life where you are. Then, in place of all the other pleasures, bring in this one: the pleasure of knowing that you are obeying God, that you are carrying out the part of a good and noble man not in word but in deed.

CXXXIV. To a good man nothing is evil, living or dead. "What then, when he does not provide food?" What else but that, like a good general, he has sounded the recall for me? I obey, I follow, speaking well of my commander and singing hymns to his works. For I came when it seemed good to him, and I go again when it seems good to him; and while I lived this was my work, to sing hymns to God, both by myself and to one man and to many.

CXXXV. Do you reflect, then, that the head and sum of all man's evils, of his meanness of spirit and his cowardice, is not death but rather the fear of death? Train yourself against this, then. Let all your reasoning, all your exercises, all your reading point here, and you will know that this is the only way men are set free.

divergences.phrase: οὐκέτι οὖν ἔσομαι; — οὐκ ἔσει· ἀλλ' ἄλλο τι, οὗ νῦν ὁ κόσμος χρείαν ἔχει
divergences.older: "Shall I then no longer be?" "Not so; thou wilt be; but something different" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "So I will no longer exist?" "You will not; but something else will, which the universe now needs."
divergences.note: Schenkl's text has a flat no: you will not be, but something else will, made of what you were. Crossley follows an emended text that softens it into survival in another form. Marcus Aurelius read the passage the hard way too (Meditations XI.35: "changes, not into nothing, but into something that does not yet exist"). "Words of bad omen" is the Lectio Meditations' phrase for δύσφημα (XI.34), kept here.

The word is the army's: the man sent ahead to see where the enemy is and come back with a true report, which is exactly what the next sentences describe. "Spy" now suggests secrecy and deceit. Diogenes' reply to Philip, "I am a scout of your greed", is the story Epictetus has in mind.

divergences.phrase: ὅς γε καὶ ἐγάμει … καὶ τοὺς παῖδας ἀπέλειπεν
divergences.older: "Nor did the hero weep and lament at leaving his children orphans." (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "Heracles married, too, where the moment seemed right to him, and had children, and left his children behind …"
divergences.note: The saying begins in the middle of a Greek sentence, at a relative pronoun whose antecedent, Heracles, stands in the sentence before, outside Crossley's extract. Crossley wrote "the hero"; Lectio gives the name, which is the only word in the paragraph not in the Greek of the extract, and gives the whole relative clause, including the marrying, which Crossley dropped.
